hints: Look across Period 3 from Mg to Si and think about what happens to nuclear charge and atomic size.
Remember that $\text{Mg}$ is $1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2$ and $\text{Si}$ is $1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^2$, so check which comparisons are actually true first.
For ions, compare $\text{Si}^{4+}$ and $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ electron counts and then see how proton number controls the pull on those same electrons.
walkthrough:
**Recall the positions and structures**

Both Mg and Si are in Period 3. Mg is Group 2 with configuration $[\text{Ne}]3s^2$. Si is Group 14 with configuration $[\text{Ne}]3s^2 3p^2$.

This means nuclear charge increases from Mg (+12) to Si (+14), while electrons are added to the same shell.

**Apply periodic trends for atoms**

Across a period, greater nuclear charge pulls the same shell in more strongly, so atomic radius decreases.

$$\text{atomic radius: Mg > Si}$$

Si also forms a giant covalent lattice with a very high melting point, while Mg has metallic bonding with a lower melting point. Si is a semiconductor, so it conducts less well than metallic Mg.

**Test rows A, B and C**

Row A comparison is false because Si is smaller than Mg, even though its explanation about 3p electrons is true.

Row B comparison is true, but its explanation is false because Si does not have delocalised electrons. Its four outer electrons are locked in localised covalent bonds.

Row C comparison is false because Si has a higher melting point than Mg, even though its explanation about bonding types is true.

**Confirm row D with isoelectronic ions**

Remove electrons to form the ions:
$$\text{Si}^{4+}: 14 - 4 = 10 \text{ electrons}$$
$$\text{Mg}^{2+}: 12 - 2 = 10 \text{ electrons}$$
Both have the $1s^2 2s^2 2p^6$ configuration, so they are isoelectronic. With more protons, $\text{Si}^{4+}$ exerts a stronger pull, so it is smaller. Both the comparison and the explanation are true and correctly linked.

options.A: Comparison is false. Atomic radius decreases across Period 3 from Mg to Si because nuclear charge increases from +12 to +14. The explanation is true ($\text{Si}$ does use 3p, $\text{Mg}$ only 3s in its outer shell) but it actually explains why Si is smaller, not larger.
options.B: Comparison is true ($\text{Mg}$ is a good metallic conductor, $\text{Si}$ is only a semiconductor) but the explanation is false. Mg contributes its 2 outer electrons to a delocalised sea, while the 4 outer electrons of Si are localised in covalent bonds, not delocalised. More delocalised electrons does not mean Si conducts better here.
options.C: Comparison is false. Si has a giant covalent structure with many strong covalent bonds to break, giving a very high melting point (about 1414 C). Mg has metallic bonding with a lower melting point (about 650 C). The bonding description is correct, but the melting point conclusion is backwards.
options.D: Both parts are true and linked. $\text{Si}^{4+}$ and $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ are both isoelectronic with 10 electrons ($1s^2 2s^2 2p^6$). Si has the greater nuclear charge (+14 versus +12), so it pulls those same 10 electrons in more strongly, making $\text{Si}^{4+}$ smaller than $\text{Mg}^{2+}$.
